title: The pilgrims turned back
hookLine: fourteen hundred set out as pilgrims for Mecca; the Prophet's camel kneels and won't go on, and they are stopped at the well of Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari)

cards: This time they aren't marching to a battle. They're going on pilgrimage.
Sahih al-Bukhari describes them setting out from Medina with their sacrificial animals garlanded and marked, and entering the state of ihram, the pilgrim's state, on the road.

Al-Bara, who was there, says they were fourteen hundred. The goal is the Ka'bah, the house they have faced in prayer from far away. And then, close to Mecca, the Prophet's camel kneels down in the road and won't get up.

teach.b: The camel's name is al-Qaswa, and in Bukhari's long report the people around her start saying: al-Qaswa has turned stubborn. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ answers: she hasn't, that isn't her nature.

teach.h: HELD BACK BY THE ONE WHO HELD BACK THE ELEPHANT.
teach.b: She has been held back by the One who held back the elephant: a reference to Surah al-Fil, the army with the elephant that never reached the Ka'bah. A stopped animal, and he reads it as a sign: not this way, not by force.
Then he says what sets the tone for everything after: by the One in whose hand is my soul, if they ask me for any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred, I will grant it.
He turns the camel and they camp at Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, by a well with very little water. Al-Bara tells what happened there. They drew the well until it was dry.
The Prophet sat at its edge, asked for some water, rinsed his mouth, made a supplication, and poured it back into the well. After a while, he says, the well gave enough for them and their animals.
So here they are: pilgrims in ihram, water in the well, and a closed door ahead. The Meccans will not let them in. A pledge, a treaty and an argument over a single word are coming.
Today is only the stopping. Much of this week has been about stopping: archers who should have stayed, defenders who held their ground, a man who held his arrow.
And now a whole caravan, halted at the edge.

how: Muslims setting out for hajj or umrah enter ihram at set points on the road, as the pilgrims of Hudaybiyyah did, and the story of the journey is taught in sirah classes.

o: the well where the pilgrims were stopped near Mecca
the city where the Prophet was born and raised
the mountain cave where the first revelation came

games.q: The pilgrims turned back — tap the pairs.
p: the camel that knelt and wouldn't go on
held back too, in Surah al-Fil
the pilgrim's state, entered on the road

s: they set out from Medina as an army to take Mecca
they set out as pilgrims, in ihram, with their sacrificial animals garlanded.
the Prophet ﷺ said al-Qaswa had turned stubborn
he said she hadn't; she was held back by the One who held back the elephant.
the well at Hudaybiyyah ran dry
al-Bara says they drew it dry, and after the Prophet poured water back in, it gave enough for all.

games.q: you're riding toward Mecca as a pilgrim, and your camel kneels in the road and won't move. the people around you say she's stubborn. what do you do?
o: force her up and ride on.
read it as a sign, and turn aside.
walk the rest of the way on foot.
games.why: he said she was held back by the One who held back the elephant, promised to grant any plan that honored the sacred, and camped at Hudaybiyyah.

practice: Bring to mind one door that's closed to you right now, a job that went to someone else, a plan the world said no to, and picture yourself at its edge, ready, with your hand resting on it instead of pushing.
Then turn around and look for the well: what's here, where you are, that you haven't drawn from yet. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you the well.

wordCard.voice: Hudaybiyyah, the well at the edge of the sacred land where the pilgrim caravan, in ihram for the Ka'bah, was stopped. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Hudaybiyyah, the name of the place and its well at the edge of the sacred land near Mecca.

carryVoice: Your line: stopped at the edge. The camel knelt, and he read it as a sign. That's day seven hundred eighty-four.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731–2732 (the garlanded animals and ihram; al-Qaswa kneels; held back by the One who held back the elephant; 'any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred')
Sahih al-Bukhari 4150 (al-Bara: fourteen hundred at Hudaybiyyah; the well drawn dry and filled again)
Qur'an 105 (Surah al-Fil: the army of the elephant)
